subject: ENG
label: Grade 01
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 01 English, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 8 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.
standard: Each unit: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school. Course pass: no unit at 'Not yet' after one retry, and a pass in SA1 and SA2.

modules.title: Letter sounds and phonics set 1
modules.outcome: hear, say and match the 26 letter sounds and blend three-letter words
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Letter sounds and phonics set 1', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: hear, say and match the 26 letter sounds and blend three-letter words. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Letter sounds and phonics set 1' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: hear, say and match the 26 letter sounds and blend three-letter words, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Echo: sound at 340 m/s returns after 2 s, so it travelled 680 m there and back, and the wall is 340 m away. Method: Model run for 'Letter sounds and phonics set 1'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Hear, say and match the 26 letter sounds and blend three-letter words: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Say the first sounds with a picture. s for sun, a for ant, t for tap, p for pin, i for ink, n for net. Say the sound, not the letter name: "sss", not "ess". Reason: sounds, not names, build words.
Step 2, Blend three sounds into a word. s-a-t: touch each letter, say each sound, then slide them together: "sat". Reason: touching and sliding keeps the child going left to right.
Step 3, Swap one sound to make a new word. sat, pat, pan, pin. Only one sound changes each time. Reason: noticing which letter changed shows how each sound matters.
Step 4, Fix an error. The child reads "pin" as "pan". Correction: look at the middle letter. The letter i says "i" as in ink. Point to it and blend again: p-i-n, "pin".

Step 5, Say the sounds in order: a, b, c, d, e, f... as sounds: "a" as in apple, "b" as in ball, "c" as in cat. Match each letter card to a picture card. Reason: matching practises both sound and shape.

Step 6, Write and say a sentence with blended words: "A cat sat on a mat." Point to each word as you read. Words to blend: c-a-t, s-a-t, m-a-t. Reason: reading a real sentence gives the sounds a purpose.
Step 7, Your turn. Blend these words: "tip", "nap", "tin". Model answer: t-i-p "tip"; n-a-p "nap"; t-i-n "tin". Now make a new word by changing the first sound of "tin" to "p": "pin".

modules.title: Reading simple words
modules.outcome: read common short words and decode simple regular words
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Reading simple words', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: read common short words and decode simple regular words. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Reading simple words' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: read common short words and decode simple regular words, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Blend c-a-t = cat, d-o-g = dog, s-u-n = sun. A name starts with a capital letter: Sara. Method: Model run for 'Reading simple words'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Read common short words and decode simple regular words: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Read tricky words you cannot sound out by sight. Words like "the", "is", "was", "you", "said". Say them, cover them, and say them again. Reason: these common words are used in nearly every sentence.
Step 2, Decode a regular word. Word: "frog". Say each sound: f-r-o-g. Blend the first two: "fr", add "o", add "g": "frog". Reason: blends like fr, st and cl are read as two sounds quickly together.
Step 3, Read a short sentence with both types. "The frog is on a log." Sight words: "the", "is", "on", "a". Decodable words: "frog", "log". Point and read smoothly.

Step 4, Fix an error. The child reads "was" as "wass". Correction: "was" is a sight word and says "woz". Practise by covering and reading it five times quickly. Reason: not every word follows the sound rule.
Step 5, Check meaning after reading. Sentence: "The dog ran to the pond." Question: "Where did the dog run?" Answer: "To the pond." Reason: reading is understanding, not only sounding out.

Step 6, Read a two-sentence story. "A big ant sat on a leaf. The ant said, 'I am hot.'" Notice speech marks around what the ant says. Point to the full stop at the end of each sentence and take a short pause.
Step 7, Your turn. Read this and answer: "The cat is on the bed. It is big." What is on the bed? Model answer: "The cat is on the bed." Then say how big it is: "It is big."

modules.title: Writing letters and my name
modules.outcome: form letters correctly and write my first name and short labels
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Writing letters and my name', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: form letters correctly and write my first name and short labels. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Writing letters and my name' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: form letters correctly and write my first name and short labels, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Blend c-a-t = cat, d-o-g = dog, s-u-n = sun. A name starts with a capital letter: Sara. Method: Model run for 'Writing letters and my name'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Form letters correctly and write my first name and short labels: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Form letters from the right starting point. The letter c starts at the top right, curves left round and stops. The letter a starts the same way and then draws a straight line down. Say the path aloud as you write.
Step 2, Keep letters the right height. Tall letters (b, d, h, l) reach the top line; short letters (a, c, e, o) sit in the middle. Write "bad" and check: b and d are tall, a is short.
Step 3, Write your first name with one capital letter. Model: "Nora". The capital N is tall, the other letters are small. Reason: names always start with a capital letter.

Step 4, Fix an error. The child writes "nora" or "NORA". Correction: "Nora", capital first, lowercase after. Another error: letter b facing backwards. Fix: draw the straight line first, then the circle to its right ("bat and ball").
Step 5, Leave spaces between words. Write "my cat" with a finger-width gap between the words. Reason: gaps make the words easy to read, and a finger space gives the correct size.
Step 6, Write labels for pictures. A picture of a hat: label "hat". A picture of a dog: label "dog". Say the sounds as you write: h-a-t. Reason: saying the sounds helps you spell the word.
Step 7, Your turn. Write your name and a label for a drawing of a sun. Model answer: "Nora" at the top, and under the sun picture write "sun".

modules.title: Simple sentences
modules.outcome: say and write a sentence that starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Simple sentences', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: say and write a sentence that starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Simple sentences' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: say and write a sentence that starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Picture of a boy with a kite. 'A boy has a kite. The kite is red. The wind is strong. He is happy.' Four connected sentences, each ending in a full stop. Method: Model run for 'Simple sentences'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Say and write a sentence that starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, A sentence tells a whole idea. Say it aloud: The cat sat. That is a sentence because it tells who and what happened. The red hat is not a sentence because it does not tell us what happens. Clap once for each word in The cat sat, and count 3 words.

Step 2, A sentence starts with a capital letter. Write The cat sat. with a big T. The word I is always a capital, too: I see a dog. Compare the big letter T with the small letter t, and trace both with your finger before you write them.

Step 3, A sentence ends with a full stop. The full stop is a small dot on the line after the last word. Write: I see a dog. Say the sentence, then put the dot straight after dog without a gap. The dot tells the reader to stop and take a breath.

Step 4, Put the words in the right order. Dog the runs is mixed up. Move the words so it makes sense: The dog runs. Then add the capital T and the full stop. Say each word in turn and point to it as you write, leaving a finger space between words.

Step 5, Say it and then write it. Say: We play in the park. Hold up one finger for each word: We, play, in, the, park. That is 5 words. Write each word with a finger space, start with a capital W, and finish with a full stop. Read it back.
Step 6, Your turn: fix this sentence, my mum can cook, and write it correctly. Answer: My mum can cook. It starts with a capital M and ends with a full stop.

modules.title: Naming words
modules.outcome: sort words for people, animals, places and things
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Naming words', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: sort words for people, animals, places and things. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Naming words' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: sort words for people, animals, places and things, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: In 'The cat sat on the mat', cat and mat are naming words (nouns). Method: Model run for 'Naming words'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Sort words for people, animals, places and things: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Sort naming words into four groups: people, animals, places, things. People: teacher, mother. Animals: cat, goat. Places: school, shop. Things: book, ball. Reason: a noun names someone or something.
Step 2, Say a sentence for each group. "The teacher is kind." "The cat is soft." "The school is big." "The ball is red." Reason: the noun is the main word in each sentence.
Step 3, Use "a" or "an" before a noun. "a cat", "a school", "an egg", "an animal". Reason: "an" goes before a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u), and "a" goes before other sounds.
Step 4, Make more than one with -s. One dog, two dogs. One book, three books. Reason: adding s changes a naming word from one to many. Say each pair aloud and hear the final s.

Step 5, Fix an error. The child puts "run" in the animal group. Correction: "run" is something we do; it is not a thing or animal. Put "dog" there. Ask: "Can I see it, touch it, or name it as a place or person?"
Step 6, Sort a mixed list. Words: mum, park, lion, pen, Sara, farm. People: mum, Sara. Places: park, farm. Animals: lion. Things: pen. Notice "Sara" begins with a capital letter because it is a name.
Step 7, Your turn. Sort: boy, tree, bus, bird, kitchen. Model answer: people: boy. Animals: bird. Places: kitchen. Things: tree, bus. Make a sentence: "The bird is in the tree."

modules.title: Action words
modules.outcome: act out and use action words in sentences
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Action words', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: act out and use action words in sentences. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Action words' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: act out and use action words in sentences, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: 'The girl runs.' Add describing words: 'The tall girl runs fast.' Tense: walk, walked, will walk. Method: Model run for 'Action words'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Act out and use action words in sentences: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Act out an action word. Say "jump" and jump. Say "clap" and clap. List them: run, hop, sit, eat, write. Reason: an action word tells what someone does.
Step 2, Put the action word in a sentence. "The boy runs." "The girl jumps." "I sit on a mat." Reason: every sentence needs a naming word and an action word.
Step 3, Use the right ending with one person. "The dog runs." "The cat sleeps." For more than one: "The dogs run." "I run." Reason: the verb takes -s after he, she, it or one thing.
Step 4, Ask a question about an action. "What does the boy do?" "He kicks the ball." Reason: "do" asks about an action, and the answer repeats the action word.

Step 5, Fix an error. Wrong: "The boy run." Right: "The boy runs." Another error: "The cat jump high." Right: "The cat jumps high." Listen to the s sound at the end when one thing is doing the action.
Step 6, Make a sentence from a word bank. Words: "The bird" and "flies", "sings", "eats". Model: "The bird flies." "The bird sings." "The bird eats." Check each has a capital letter and a full stop.
Step 7, Your turn. Write two sentences using the action words swim and read. Model answer: "The fish swims." "I read a book." Check: capital letter, action word, full stop.

modules.title: Rhymes and short stories
modules.outcome: retell a story with beginning, middle and end and join in with rhymes
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Rhymes and short stories', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: retell a story with beginning, middle and end and join in with rhymes. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Rhymes and short stories' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: retell a story with beginning, middle and end and join in with rhymes, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: cat, hat and mat rhyme. Make a couplet: 'The sun is high, a bird can fly.' High and fly rhyme. Method: Model run for 'Rhymes and short stories'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Retell a story with beginning, middle and end and join in with rhymes: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Retell a short story in three parts. Story: "A hen found a seed. She planted it. It grew into a big tree." Beginning: the hen finds a seed. Middle: she plants it. End: a tree grows.
Step 2, Use story words. "First, the hen found a seed. Next, she planted it. At the end, a tree grew." Reason: first, next and at the end show the order of events.
Step 3, Join in with a rhyme. "Hen, ten" and "tree, three" rhyme because they share the end sound. Say: "One hen, two hens, three hens, ten." Clap the beat as you say it.
Step 4, Find rhyming words. Pairs: cat and hat, bug and rug, star and car. Reason: the end sounds match, even if the spelling differs a little.
Step 5, Fix an error. The child tells the end before the middle. Correction: ask "What happened first? What happened next? How did it end?" Reason: events must follow the order of the story.

Step 6, Draw and say three pictures. Picture 1: a boy with a kite. Picture 2: the kite flies high. Picture 3: the kite gets stuck in a tree. Retell: "The boy has a kite. It flies high. It gets stuck."
Step 7, Your turn. Retell this: "A cat sat on a wall. It saw a bird. The bird flew away." Model answer: "First, the cat sat on a wall. Next, it saw a bird. At the end, the bird flew away."

modules.title: Speaking and listening
modules.outcome: take turns, listen to instructions and speak in a full sentence
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Speaking and listening', taught in a way that is short, playful, with objects, pictures and talk. The target is clear: take turns, listen to instructions and speak in a full sentence. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Speaking and listening' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: take turns, listen to instructions and speak in a full sentence, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Retell in order with first, next, then, last. Ask: 'What happened next?' Reply politely: 'Thank you, I agree because...' Method: Model run for 'Speaking and listening'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 20 to 30 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: one page in your learning book.
modules.standard: Take turns, listen to instructions and speak in a full sentence: at least 4 of 5 attempts correct, said or written, with one real example from home or school.
steps: Step 1, Take turns when talking. Rule: one person speaks, the others listen. Model: "It is your turn, Sam." "Thank you. I like red." Reason: waiting for your turn shows respect.
Step 2, Listen to a two-step instruction. Teacher: "Pick up your pencil and write your name." Do two actions in order: first pick up, then write. Reason: listening carefully means doing every step.

Step 3, Answer in a full sentence. Question: "What is your favourite food?" Answer: "My favourite food is rice." Not just "Rice." Reason: a full sentence has a naming word and an action or being word.
Step 4, Speak so people can hear. Use a loud, clear voice and look at the listener. Model: "Good morning. My name is Ana." Reason: a clear voice and eye contact make you easier to understand.
Step 5, Fix an error. Question: "Where do you live?" Child: "Near." Better: "I live near the market." Another error: speaking while someone else is talking. Correction: wait, then say "Excuse me."
Step 6, Ask a question back. "I like cats. Do you like cats?" Answer: "Yes, I do." Reason: a question keeps a conversation going.
Step 7, Your turn. Answer in a full sentence: "What do you do after school?" Model answer: "After school I play with my friends." Then ask a question: "What do you do after school?"

rubric: Explains the idea to someone else
Practises most days and keeps evidence
checks: Unit 1 (Letter sounds and phonics set 1): Blend these words: "tip", "nap", "tin".
t-i-p "tip"; n-a-p "nap"; t-i-n "tin". Now make a new word by changing the first sound of "tin" to "p": "pin". (Covered in unit 1: Letter sounds and phonics set 1.)
Unit 2 (Reading simple words): Read this and answer: "The cat is on the bed. It is big." What is on the bed?.
"The cat is on the bed." Then say how big it is: "It is big." (Covered in unit 2: Reading simple words.)
Unit 3 (Writing letters and my name): Write your name and a label for a drawing of a sun.
"Nora" at the top, and under the sun picture write "sun". (Covered in unit 3: Writing letters and my name.)
Unit 4 (Simple sentences): Fix this sentence, my mum can cook, and write it correctly.
My mum can cook. It starts with a capital M and ends with a full stop. (Covered in unit 4: Simple sentences.)
Unit 5 (Naming words): Sort: boy, tree, bus, bird, kitchen.
people: boy. Animals: bird. Places: kitchen. Things: tree, bus. Make a sentence: "The bird is in the tree." (Covered in unit 5: Naming words.)
Unit 6 (Action words): Write two sentences using the action words swim and read.
"The fish swims." "I read a book." Check: capital letter, action word, full stop. (Covered in unit 6: Action words.)
Unit 7 (Rhymes and short stories): Retell this: "A cat sat on a wall. It saw a bird. The bird flew away.".
"First, the cat sat on a wall. Next, it saw a bird. At the end, the bird flew away." (Covered in unit 7: Rhymes and short stories.)
Unit 8 (Speaking and listening): Answer in a full sentence: "What do you do after school?".
"After school I play with my friends." Then ask a question: "What do you do after school?" (Covered in unit 8: Speaking and listening.)

Word: "frog". Say each sound: f-r-o-g. Blend the first two: "fr", add "o", add "g": "frog". Reason: blends like fr, st and cl are read as two sounds quickly together. (Covered in unit 2: Reading simple words.)
ladder: L1: say and read familiar words and short sentences.
L2: read short texts and write connected sentences.
L3: write paragraphs and speak on a topic with notes.
L4: write for different purposes and analyse how texts persuade.
L5: write and argue at length; handle unseen texts.
L6 (degree): academic reading, writing and citation.
L7 (postgraduate): publish, teach or translate with expert accuracy.
